executive_summary: USD/JPY trades at 157.68 (6 August close), meaning one US dollar buys 157.68 yen; a falling pair means the yen is strengthening. The pair has fallen 2.78% over one month, 1.25% over three months and 1.54% over six months, and sits at the 71st percentile of a 52-week range spanning 142.11 to 164.088 — the high having been printed on 26 July, a four-decade extreme, just four sessions before the market broke. The dominant bilateral narrative is no longer the rate differential: it is the emergence of a coordinated official ceiling. Japan's MoF sold an estimated JPY 8.45trn on 30 July, and Japan's Finance Ministry confirmed it had conducted a coordinated yen-buying operation with the U.S. Treasury, signalling it 'will not hesitate to conduct further coordinated interventions in the future'. That is the single most important bilateral fact in this report and it exists in neither standalone dossier: Treasury Secretary Bessent opted to sell euros rather than dollars, to shore up the yen without weakening the greenback — a design that explicitly severs a bearish USD/JPY view from the mildly bullish broad-USD view in the base dossier. The USD dossier is Bullish USD at conviction 2 (trade-weighted carry of +147bp); the JPY dossier is Bullish JPY at conviction 4 tactically. Those views are only superficially in conflict, because the dollar's carry advantage is concentrated against EUR/CHF/CAD while the pair-specific policy architecture is now aimed squarely at USD/JPY. We are Bearish USD/JPY on both horizons — tactical conviction 3 (weighted score −0.2999), strategic conviction 3 (−0.2484) — targeting 155.00 over two to four weeks and 152.00 over one to six months, against a six-month forward of 155.15. The caveat is unambiguous: the pair still pays 262.5bp of annualised carry to be short, both prior 2026 intervention episodes were fully retraced, and a Fed hike on 16 September against a BoJ hold on 18 September would re-widen the gap to 287.5bp and break the thesis inside a single week.

market_context.valuation_assessment: The bilateral valuation gap is the widest in the entire G10 matrix. The base dossier's relative-REER derivation places the dollar 6.83% expensive versus the yen, implying fair value near USD/JPY 148.39; the quote dossier's mirror computation places the yen 6.8% cheap to the dollar with an implied 147.74. The two derivations agree to within 65 pips, which is unusual and raises confidence in the sign. Underneath that, Japan's BIS real broad effective rate at 65.30 for June 2026 is the lowest reading ever recorded on the series and sits 7.82% below its own 30-month mean, while the dollar's REER at 107.84 is within roughly one percent of its own five-year average on either of two competing derivations. So this is not two stretched currencies netting out — it is a fairly valued dollar against a record-cheap yen. Institutionally, this matters because Japanese corporates are not planning for it: the June Tankan FY2026 planning assumption is 152.57 and the ten major life insurers assume 154, both materially stronger than spot, so a move toward 152–154 forces no adverse revision but validates existing hedge programmes. What is priced at 157.68 is a permanent 6–7% real discount on the yen; what is not priced is any mechanism to close it. The joint intervention is that mechanism, and it did not exist a week ago.

market_context.recent_regime: Through 26 July the regime was a low-volatility carry grind in which USD/JPY ground to a 40-year high on a 262.5bp differential and one-month implied volatility below 6.0, with speculators adding to a record short yen position into the top. That regime ended on 30 July with unadvertised MoF intervention and was institutionalised on 31 July–1 August when the U.S. Treasury bought yen, marking Washington's first yen-buying intervention with Tokyo in more than a decade, with the New York Fed selling euros for yen through Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. The dollar had risen in recent weeks to nearly 164 yen, its highest since 1986, and Japan may have sold as much as $58.97 billion to buy yen on Thursday. The operative regime for the next month is therefore a defended range: the market must decide whether a two-government bid is a durable ceiling or a liquidity event to be faded, and the resolution runs through the 18 September BoJ meeting.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Carry was working spectacularly and is now at maximum vulnerability. The precondition — suppressed implied volatility, record spec shorts, records in global equities, HY OAS at 284bp — is precisely the configuration that precedes a disorderly unwind, and the 30 July session delivered the largest one-day dollar decline against the yen since 2022. Carry is not broken: it still pays roughly 22bp a month to hold the pair long. But it is now being earned against a two-government official bid and a vol surface that has repriced, which converts a benign accrual into a negatively convex one. Using the last observed implied volatility of 6.36, the carry-to-vol ratio is 0.41; using current ~10% realised, it falls to 0.26, a roughly 37% deterioration in the risk-adjusted proposition in a week with no change in the nominal carry. Set against the 30 July–3 August move of 8.84 yen, the intervention erased roughly twenty-five months of accrued carry in three sessions, and the forward curve confirms covered interest parity holds, meaning the carry is not an edge for either side — the edge is entirely in the spot path relative to that curve.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is 262.5bp — Fed funds midpoint 3.625% against a BoJ target of 'around 1.0 percent' — and it is the widest gap in the DXY basket. The trajectory, however, is unambiguously one-directional: the Fed has been on hold all year with a June SEP median implying one hike, while the BoJ has delivered 100bp of cumulative tightening and carries a standing dissent for 1.25%. The pricing asymmetry is the tactical point. Prediction-market pricing puts 77.5% on no change and 23.5% on a 25bp increase at the September BoJ meeting, while a TONA-futures bootstrap puts the market-implied probability of no change at 62% for the 17 September meeting — a 23.5% to 38% spread between two public representations of the same event, which is itself evidence that BoJ front-end pricing is poorly anchored. Against that, the BoJ held steady in July while signalling that upside risks could justify another hike as early as September. On the sovereign curve the bilateral gaps are 278bp at two years and 195bp at ten years, and the ten-year gap has compressed roughly 95bp over twelve months. The transmission to the pair runs through the two-year, not the ten-year: the two-year gap is the true measure of the carry penalty and it compresses only if the BoJ out-hikes the Fed. Neither central bank meets inside the tactical window, so the tactical signal is entirely a repricing signal, driven by the 10 August Summary of Opinions and the 20 August national CPI. Confidence is held to 50 precisely because the two public probability sources disagree by 15 percentage points and because a Fed hike on 16 September is a live offset.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential compresses mechanically under any reasonable path. Japan is the only economy in the pair whose policy rate sits below its own central bank's estimate of neutral — 1.00% against a stated ~2% — implying roughly 100bp of latent tightening, while the Fed at 3.625% is at or above neutral and constrained by a Q2 GDP print of +1.5% annualised. Board member Tamura has argued the BoJ should continue raising rates at intervals of a few months, with the policy rate gradually moving toward a neutral level of around 2%. If the BoJ delivers 50bp by end-Q1 2027 and the Fed delivers 25bp, the gap narrows from 262.5bp to 237.5bp; if the Fed holds, it narrows to 212.5bp. Either path reduces the carry cushion on a long pair position by 10–20% while the pair-specific volatility floor has already risen. Corroborating the direction, projections assuming the BoJ raises to 1.00–1.25% and the Fed settles at 3.50–3.75% imply the differential compresses toward 250–275bp by Q4. The transmission to spot is the two-year gap and the hedged-return channel: at a 278bp front-end gap, Japanese institutions face hedging costs that already erase the entire pickup on hedged Treasuries, which is why the repatriation flow in Factor 4 is live. The genuine strategic risk is the disconfirming evidence — the ten-year gap compressed 95bp over twelve months and the pair rose anyway — so compression is necessary but demonstrably not sufficient.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is +165bp in the dollar's favour on core measures (US core PCE 3.3% versus Japan core CPI 1.6%), but the momentum differential runs the other way and momentum is what moves the pair. US core CPI has decelerated from 2.9% to 2.6% and the Dallas Fed trimmed mean is only 2.2%, so the US overshoot is narrow and energy-driven; Japan's Tokyo July core printed 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, and Tokyo leads the national series by roughly a month, so the 20 August national print is likely to accelerate from 1.6% toward 1.8%. The growth differential is +178bp in the dollar's favour on year-on-year GDP, but again the direction of travel diverges: US Q2 annualised growth slowed to 1.5% from 2.1% with June payrolls of just 57,000 and 74,000 of downward back revisions, while Japan's June Tankan showed large manufacturers at +22, the highest since 2018, and the July flash composite PMI at 53.1. Asymmetric sensitivity favours the Japanese leg for the next four weeks: the US calendar delivers payrolls and CPI, both partially anticipated, while the Japanese calendar delivers a Summary of Opinions and a CPI print where consensus is anchored on a stale national reading and under-weights the Tokyo lead. The transmission is straightforward — a Japanese upside CPI surprise reprices September BoJ odds directly, and each 10-percentage-point move in that probability is worth roughly 40–60 pips on the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two economies converge in the direction that closes the pair. The US growth premium that underwrote USD/JPY through 2023–25 is eroding: US real GDP at 1.5% annualised, a three-month payroll trend near 60,000, participation falling to 61.5%, and average hourly earnings at 3.5%. Japan is doing the opposite: the 2026 shunto settled at 5.01% overall with a 3.50% base-pay component, a third consecutive year above 5%, nominal earnings above 3% for four consecutive months, and five consecutive months of positive real wages — a wage-price mechanism operating for the first time in three decades while the equivalent US mechanism decays. The inflation differential should narrow from 165bp toward 100bp or less, with the BoJ's July Outlook raising FY2027 core CPI to 2.4% and the Fed's June SEP projecting headline PCE falling to 2.3% in 2027. The BoJ maintained its policy rate at 1.00% via an 8-1 vote while upgrading its economic outlook and signalling its intention to continue rate hikes, warning that core inflation might overshoot its 2% target. The pair transmission is that convergent inflation with divergent policy starting points forces the BoJ to travel further than the Fed. The counterweight, and why confidence is 55 rather than higher, is that Japan's inflation impulse is imported — a 5.4-percentage-point wedge between 7.1% goods PPI and 1.7% core-core — so if Brent falls toward the EIA's $65 2027 forecast the Japanese leg deflates faster than the US leg.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: USD/JPY sits in the framework's moderate risk-sensitivity band, and the current environment is risk-on: the S&P 500 closed at a record 7,489.72 on 31 July, IG OAS is 80bp, HY OAS 284bp and the VIX 17.09. In a goldilocks tape the yen is the funding leg and the dollar is the destination, which is directionally pair-positive. But the bilateral nuance that distinguishes this pair from AUD/JPY is that both currencies are havens, so a risk shock produces two competing bids and the net move is far smaller and less reliable than the raw beta suggests. This cycle has an additional and unusual asymmetry: because the US is now a net energy exporter and Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil, an energy-driven risk shock delivers the dollar a haven bid and a terms-of-trade gain while delivering the yen a haven bid and a terms-of-trade loss — so the classic risk-off-is-yen-positive rule has repeatedly failed for this pair in 2026. The yen made a 40-year low during the July Hormuz escalation. The tactical read is that the current tape is mildly pair-positive and the tail which would reverse it is real but has been demonstrated not to work through the energy channel. The offsetting consideration is the pure carry-unwind channel: with 185,047 contracts of net short yen still to clear, an equity-led or credit-led shock remains the highest-beta pair-negative event available. Confidence is 50 because these two forces are genuinely close in magnitude and the classification of the next shock is unknowable.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk channel for this specific pair is genuinely two-sided and forcing a stance would add noise. The pair-positive branch requires the current record-equity, tight-credit, low-vol configuration to persist for another four to six months, which is not the base case at a 5.98 one-year EUR/USD implied vol and a 9.85% six-month USD/JPY implied against realised in the bottom decile. The pair-negative branch — a disorderly carry unwind — is the higher-beta outcome, and the yen carry trade has been one of the most important macro dynamics affecting risk assets, and when the yen suddenly strengthens those trades unwind, sometimes violently, as in the August 2024 episode. But the third branch, an energy-led shock, is pair-positive and has occurred twice in 2026 already. Three branches, two directions, comparable probabilities: Neutral is the honest classification. What we can assert without direction is that the option surface is charging too little for all three, which is why we route the strategic expression through convexity rather than spot in the Factor 9 expression assessment.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the highest-confidence factor in the report and the proximate reason for the tactical stance. The two legs of the pair are positioned in the same direction, which amplifies rather than mutes the signal: specs are net long dollars (+17,197 on the ICE index contract, and -240,642 across seven G10 futures) and net short yen (-185,047 combined leveraged and asset-manager contracts on the 28 July report, on open interest of 432,366). A long USD/JPY is therefore the most crowded single expression in the complex, and it was still being added to into the 26 July high — asset managers alone added 26,089 contracts of short yen in one week, which is capitulation into a trend rather than measured allocation. Against that inventory has now landed the largest official flow in the pair's history: Japan may have sold as much as $58.97 billion to buy yen on Thursday, and Tokyo intervened again in New York trading hours on Friday, followed by a US operation over 31 July and 1 August executed by the New York Fed through Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with reporting indicating planned scale of between $5 billion and $10 billion of yen purchases. The mechanical consequence is that a short-covering flow of 60,000–90,000 contracts is now in train, and the retail crowd — 89% short USD/JPY on 29 July — is on the other side, meaning the institutional cover has no natural counterparty at these levels. That is why we expect the 4 and 11 August COT reports to show the net short shrinking materially, and why positioning normalisation alone, with no change in any fundamental, is worth two to three yen of pair downside.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At the strategic horizon the futures overhang clears within weeks and the structural bilateral flow picture takes over — and here the pair has a channel that no other G10 pair possesses. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US Treasuries: approximately $1.19 trillion as of March 2026 on Treasury Department data. That stock is now in motion. Japanese investors sold a net ¥4.67 trillion, roughly $29.6 billion, in US government, agency and municipal bonds during Q1 2026 — the largest quarterly reduction in nearly four years — against total holdings of about $1.203 trillion, some 13% of all foreign-held US debt. The driver is bilateral and self-reinforcing: higher domestic yields mean Japanese life insurers and pension funds can now earn competitive returns at home without taking currency risk by parking money in US Treasuries. Every 25bp of BoJ tightening widens that incentive and converts a passive USD/JPY-supportive reinvestment flow into an active pair-negative repatriation flow. The offsetting negative is GPIF's May 2026 seven-percentage-point rotation out of JGBs into foreign equities, roughly USD 52bn of structural yen selling, though Finance Minister Katayama has since signalled state pension funds could rotate back toward domestic assets. Confidence is 55 rather than higher because the repatriation channel is slow, lumpy and politically contested, and because the ten major life insurers' stated FY2026 plans are defensive rather than actively repatriating.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the strongest pair-positive factor and it is a genuine bilateral asymmetry rather than a netting exercise. Applying the framework's commodity direction rules: Oil up → +USD (mild positive, net energy exporter), --JPY (strong negative). Net effect: pair RISES. And: LNG (JKM) up → --JPY, with the US a net LNG exporter. Net effect: pair RISES. Brent at $91.82 with a Gulf Coast 3-2-1 crack spread of $63.61 is a direct real-income transfer from Japan to the United States, and the magnitude is visible in the data: Japan's June mineral fuel imports were JPY 2.10trn, up 41.9% year-on-year, with petroleum import values up 59.3% while crude volumes fell 13.7% — a pure price shock. Japan's terms of trade collapsed from 88.34 in April to 83.95 in May, a 5.0% single-month deterioration against a since-1960 average of 150.50. Japan posted a second consecutive monthly goods deficit at JPY 406.9bn against a JPY 120bn consensus. The bilateral trade relationship itself is large and lopsided but slow-moving: US goods exports to Japan of $79.7bn against imports of $148.2bn (2024), a US net goods deficit of $68.5bn. That structural US deficit is a persistent, low-frequency pair-negative flow of roughly $5.7bn a month, but it is dwarfed an order of magnitude by the energy channel and by the $1.19trn portfolio stock. The tactical mitigant is that Brent has already fallen 13% from the $105.32 spike on 23 July to $91.82 on 27 July, so the marginal energy impulse has turned.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.13 strategic weight this is the largest single counterweight to the bearish thesis and it must be respected. The Strait of Hormuz has not physically normalised — fewer than ten commodity ships per day were transiting on 27 July against roughly one hundred pre-war — and ADNOC's own guidance is that full flows will not resume until 2027, so the terms-of-trade transfer from Japan to the United States has a multi-quarter tail. Structurally, Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil while the US is a net energy exporter, which means the pair carries a permanent, one-directional energy beta that no amount of policy convergence removes. The bilateral scenario arithmetic is stark: if Brent rises 10% to roughly $101, the pair gains an estimated 1.5-2.5 yen; if Brent falls 10% to roughly $83, the pair loses an estimated 1.0-2.0 yen, with the asymmetry favouring the upside because Japan's terms of trade are already 44% below their long-run average. Analysis of this specific dependency concludes that Brent at $70-80 keeps Japan's deficit manageable and allows BoJ tightening to strengthen the yen, while Brent above $90 widens the deficit and creates a floor under USD/JPY around 148-152 — which is a precise statement of why our strategic target is 152 rather than 148. The offsetting structural consideration is the US net international investment position of -$21.27trn against Japan's record net creditor position of JPY 561.75trn, but that stock imbalance has been ignored for two decades and is not a strategic-horizon driver.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are hawkish, which on a naive reading cancels. It does not, for two reasons. First, the pricing of that hawkishness is asymmetric: the Fed's is fully discounted — the 1Y bill at 4.08% against a 3.63% effective rate embeds roughly 45bp of tightening, and the 29 July 9-3 vote with three hike dissents is public — while the BoJ's is not, with September priced at 23.5-38% against a Governor who has said the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes and a sitting member already voting for 1.25%. Second, and this is the bilateral novelty, a third guidance channel has opened that sits outside both dossiers: the two finance ministries are now jointly guiding the exchange rate itself. The MoF stated the intervention was carried out in accordance with the Joint Statement of the Japanese and U.S. Finance Ministers issued in September 2025 and was aimed at addressing recent excessive volatility and disorderly movements of the yen, and Bessent confirmed that Friday's coordinated foreign exchange actions countered disorderly yen movements, adding that Treasury remains in close communication with MOF and BOJ and will not hesitate to participate further. A US Treasury that has publicly described the yen as substantially undervalued and has now put its own balance sheet behind that view is a guidance regime for this pair that did not exist ten days ago. The credibility differential also favours the yen leg at the margin: Japan's MoF confirmed it purchased yen in coordination with the U.S. Treasury, and Katayama warned authorities would not hesitate to intervene jointly again should disorderly conditions return. Sequencing matters and it favours the bear case: the Fed meets 16 September, the BoJ 18 September, so the Fed sets the tone and any Fed hold hands the initiative directly to a BoJ that has pointed at that meeting.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the question is whether both guidance regimes survive contact with their respective growth slowdowns, and whether the joint FX framework is a one-off or a standing facility. On the first, the BoJ's framework is the more durable: it is anchored on a board-stated neutral rate of around 2% against a 1.00% policy rate, and delivery of 50bp still leaves policy accommodative, whereas the Fed's hawkish framing requires holding a 3.625% rate into a decelerating economy with a 1.5% annualised Q2 and a payroll trend near 60,000. A Fed that is forced to abandon its hawkish framing does more damage to the pair than a BoJ that under-delivers by one hike, because the pair's forward curve is anchored on the level of US rates. On the second, the evidence points to a standing facility rather than a one-off: the ministry also announced plans to utilise the Federal Reserve's foreign and international monetary authorities repo facility in the future, and the FIMA repo facility allows Japan to raise dollar liquidity without outright sales of U.S. Treasuries, potentially easing funding pressures on Tokyo for intervention. That is architecture, not improvisation, and it removes the single largest historical constraint on repeated Japanese intervention. The bilateral consequence is a soft but credible policy ceiling in the 162-164 region and a materially fatter left tail for the pair. Confidence is 60 rather than higher because the same joint statement gives no floor, and because a sceptical reading holds that the yen showed signs of weakening again post-intervention and that the market will have the last word if the differential is maintained.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The tactical event set for this pair is unusually dense and, unusually, is dominated by a bilateral official binary rather than a macro one. The dominant live event is the repeat-intervention risk: two governments have now stated they will act again, the MoF's monthly disclosure covering 30 July to 27 August will confirm the true size of the operation in late August, and the market has no visible option premium for either. Set against that, the pair-positive external binary is the Hormuz Article 5 transit-fee expiry around 16 August, which — because the US is a net energy exporter and Japan imports 99% of its oil — is the one event that hits both legs in the pair-positive direction simultaneously. The bilateral clustering is what makes this factor tradeable: 7 August US payrolls, 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions, 12 August US CPI, 16 August Hormuz expiry, 19 August Japanese trade data and FOMC minutes, and 20 August Japanese CPI fall inside a fourteen-day window, with the Japanese events skewed pair-negative and the US events two-sided. Asymmetric event exposure sits on the Japanese leg: with September BoJ odds at 23.5-38% there is far more room for the Japanese calendar to move the pair than for the US calendar, where the Fed's path is already discounted. Confidence is only 52 because the two dominant binaries — intervention and Hormuz — point in opposite directions with comparable probability.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the pair's event landscape does not resolve into a direction. On the pair-negative side sit three BoJ meetings, a standing joint intervention facility now backed by FIMA dollar liquidity, and the anticipation of March fiscal-year-end repatriation from late January. On the pair-positive side sit an unresolved Hormuz situation with a multi-quarter tail, the US domestic political calendar which is dollar-negative but transmits to the pair only weakly because the yen has its own fiscal problem, and Japan's own FY2027 budget in late December under a government with a 352-seat supermajority. Bilateral political risk between the two economies is genuinely low and improving: the framework agreement leaves autos at a 15% tariff with the threatened 25% unimplemented, Japan has committed up to $550bn of funding for US strategic-sector investment, and the February 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling removed the largest legal overhang. There is no live trade dispute between these two countries capable of moving the pair — which is itself notable and distinguishes USD/JPY from USD/CAD or USD/CNH. Neutral is the honest classification.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For once, both sovereigns are deteriorating in the same direction and at comparable pace, which nets to a genuine Neutral rather than a lazy one. The US 30-year closed 31 July at 5.27%, the highest of 2026, with 10-year breakevens flat at 2.28% — a pure term-premium repricing, which is dollar-negative and therefore pair-negative. Japan's 30-year sits at 3.971%, within 4bp of an all-time high of 4.013% set on 9 July, with the FY2026 budget a record JPY 122.3trn and central-plus-local debt revised to 187.6% of GDP — which is yen-negative and therefore pair-positive. Both long ends are being repriced for fiscal reasons rather than growth or policy, and in both cases that repricing has been currency-negative for the respective issuer. The 30-year spread is +130bp in the dollar's favour and has been roughly stable, so the differential is not generating a directional signal at a two-to-four-week horizon. The one bilateral linkage worth noting is unusual and runs through the intervention: a plausible reading of the joint operation is that Washington acted partly to avoid Japan becoming a forced seller of Treasuries. Severe instability in the yen can spill into global bond markets, particularly if Japan needs to sell part of its substantial U.S. Treasury holdings to finance intervention. That linkage makes the two fiscal positions mutually reinforcing rather than competing, which is precisely why neither dominates.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the marginal fiscal deterioration is on the Japanese side and it is the mechanism by which higher Japanese yields have coincided with a weaker yen throughout 2026 — the disconfirming fact that most damages a naive rate-compression thesis. Prime Minister Takaichi's LDP-Ishin coalition holds 352 of 465 lower-house seats on an expansionary platform, delivered a supplementary budget in May, and the FY2027 budget and JGB issuance plan land in late December inside this horizon. Japan is entering the first period in three decades in which rising rates cost the sovereign real money: debt-service costs of JPY 31.3trn on a 3.0% assumption, a 29-year high, against a debt stock at 187.6% of GDP, while the BoJ's holdings fall from JPY 518trn toward a projected JPY 480trn by end-March 2027. The US position is worse in trajectory but better in structure — a 5.8%-of-GDP deficit and a judicially removed $1.7trn of projected tariff revenue against a reserve-currency status that has never been tested at these levels. The bilateral judgement is that Japan's fiscal channel is the faster-moving one at the margin, because Japan is repricing a thirty-year regime change while the US is repricing a familiar deficit, and because the joint intervention has explicitly capped one of the yen's channels while leaving the fiscal channel wide open. Confidence is only 48 because the direction of travel on the US 30-year is equally adverse and the spread has been stable.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is a USD-base pair, so the funding channel transmits directly, and domestic dollar liquidity has become genuinely scarce. Reserve balances fell to $2,944,541mn on 29 July, down $355.2bn year-on-year; the ON RRP is effectively drained at roughly $2bn; the TGA is at $997.9bn; and SOFR printed 3.65% on 30 July, exactly at IORB and 2bp above an effective funds rate of 3.63%, with a 75th percentile of 3.70%. Scarce dollars with no buffer is historically pair-positive, because it raises the marginal cost of being short the dollar. The bilateral funding channel that would work the other way — a widening negative JPY/USD cross-currency basis forcing Japanese repatriation — remains unmeasurable this cycle, and its absence is the reason confidence is capped at 48. Offsetting the scarcity story is a pair-specific development with no analogue elsewhere: the MoF's stated intention to use the Fed's FIMA repo facility means Japanese official dollar demand can now be met without either selling Treasuries or bidding in the FX market, which removes a source of dollar demand that would otherwise have been pair-positive during intervention episodes. Net, the domestic scarcity signal is real but modest and the FIMA offset is specific to this pair, producing a low-confidence Bullish reading.

The two standalone dossiers appear to conflict — the USD dossier is Bullish USD at conviction 2, the JPY dossier is Bullish JPY at conviction 4 — but the conflict is superficial and its resolution is the central bilateral insight of this report: the dollar's carry advantage is trade-weighted and concentrated against EUR, CHF, CAD and SEK, which together are 74.5% of the DXY, while the pair-specific policy architecture is now aimed squarely at USD/JPY. Bessent's decision to sell euros rather than dollars was explicitly designed to shore up the yen without weakening the greenback — a structure that permits a broadly firm dollar and a falling USD/JPY simultaneously, and which no standalone dossier can generate. The bilateral-specific factors that modify the standalone views are therefore three: the joint official ceiling (Factor 6), the amplification of positioning by same-direction crowding on both legs (Factor 4), and the pair-unique repatriation channel running through Japan's $1.19trn Treasury stock (Factor 4 strategic). What is priced versus what we expect: the market prices a September BoJ hike at 23.5-38%, prices the intervention as a fadeable liquidity event, and sells the pair's gamma at sub-7 implied against ~10 realised. We expect the 20 August national CPI to print core at 1.8% or above following a 20bp Tokyo beat, and we assess fair value for September at 45-50%. The path of least resistance over the next four weeks is lower, but grudgingly so: spot has closed in a 55-pip band for four sessions directly beneath the 200-day, which is a coil rather than a trend. strategic.rationale: At strategic weights four factors carry 0.64 of the total — Policy & Rates at 0.27, Guidance at 0.14, External Balance at 0.13 and USD Funding at 0.10 — and the bearish case rests overwhelmingly on the first two. The weighted score of -0.2484 implies a directional view held with genuine humility, because the concentration is high: remove Factor 1 and the score collapses to -0.0864, a near-flat reading. The reinforcing interaction is between Factors 1, 4 and 6. A BoJ that is 100bp below its own neutral estimate keeps tightening; each 25bp of tightening narrows the 278bp two-year gap and widens the domestic-versus-hedged-Treasury return advantage for Japanese institutions; and higher domestic yields mean Japanese life insurers and pension funds can earn competitive returns at home without taking currency risk by parking money in US Treasuries, converting a passive pair-supportive reinvestment flow into an active pair-negative repatriation flow from a $1.19trn stock. That loop is self-reinforcing and is the strategic core of the thesis. The conflicting interaction is between Factors 1 and 5. Policy convergence says the pair falls; the energy terms-of-trade transfer says it rises, and the quote dossier's own analysis puts a floor under USD/JPY around 148-152 while Brent stays above $90. Those two are not resolvable analytically — they are resolved by oil, and our 152.00 strategic target is deliberately set at the top of that estimated floor rather than below it. What is priced versus what we expect: aggregated forecasts have USD/JPY at 159.32 late 2026 and 156.31 early 2027, and the six-month forward outright is 155.15. We expect 152.00 at six months — roughly 315 pips below the forward and 430 pips below the aggregate consensus path. The path of least resistance is a grinding, interrupted appreciation of the yen with a decision point in the middle rather than a smooth trend. The dated catalysts that decide it are the 16 September FOMC with SEP, the 18 September and 30 October BoJ meetings, the 17 August and subsequent TIC releases, the 9 December FOMC and the 18 December BoJ. Conviction drivers are the 100bp BoJ gap-to-neutral, a record-cheap yen at a BIS REER of 65.30, and a joint official framework backed by FIMA dollar liquidity. Conviction detractors are the energy terms-of-trade transfer at a 0.13 weight, Japan's own fiscal trajectory, and the demonstrated 2026 failure of the spread-compression channel. Actionability is moderate: the six-month forward at 155.15 already finances away 44% of the base-case move, so the honest strategic edge is 315 pips, not 568.

USD/JPY ranks ahead of USD/CAD, USD/SEK, USD/CHF and EUR/USD because none of those has a bilateral official framework or a 100bp central-bank gap-to-neutral. Among the yen crosses, USD/JPY drops to 4th of eight strategically, behind AUD/JPY, NZD/JPY and JPY/CHF. AUD/JPY retains the widest carry penalty and valuation gap; NZD/JPY has an actively hiking RBNZ; JPY/CHF is the only relationship where the yen earns carry — 100bp today, widening to 150bp after two BoJ hikes — making it the highest-quality relative-value structure. cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: There is no stance inflection, but there is a confidence inflection at the 16-18 September central bank sequence (FOMC 16 September, BoJ 18 September) — the tightest bilateral policy cluster of the year. cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Because the horizons agree, the position does not need to be flipped mid-horizon, which materially improves after-cost economics for a pair that costs 34.5 pips a month to hold short. The key number is whether FY2027 core CPI is revised above the current 2.4% as government energy subsidies roll off — a mechanical uplift the BoJ has itself flagged, since the July Outlook cut the FY2026 inflation forecast to 2.5% from 2.8% reflecting government energy subsidy steps.

catalysts.event: FOMC and BoJ policy meetings nine days apart, both with projections
catalysts.rationale: The Fed's final SEP of 2026 is the last opportunity to deliver its own 3.8% end-2026 median; the BoJ's meeting carries an OIS-implied post-meeting rate of 1.21%, roughly 81-84% cumulative probability of one hike delivered by year-end. If the Fed marks down its median while the BoJ delivers, the differential compresses to 212.5bp in nine days — the single largest potential bilateral repricing in the strategic window.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 budget and JGB issuance plan
catalysts.rationale: The FY2026 plan cut calendar-base market issuance by JPY 3.8trn and held new debt below JPY 30trn, which supported the long end. The FY2027 equivalent under a Takaichi government with a 352-seat supermajority is the key test of whether fiscal discipline survives the political mandate, with the 30-year JGB already at 3.971%. A loose plan pushes the JGB super-long above 4.25% and is pair-positive through the fiscal-risk-premium channel.

invalidators.condition: USD/JPY closes above the 100-day moving average at 160.24 for three consecutive sessions with no further official intervention
invalidators.mechanism: The joint operation would have been tested and dismissed by the market — the pair's entire tactical bear case rests on the credibility of a two-government ceiling, and a 250-pip recovery above the 200-day and 100-day without a response demonstrates the ceiling is verbal rather than operational, converting trend-following flow back to pair-long.

invalidators.condition: The Fed hikes 25bp on 16 September while the BoJ holds on 18 September
invalidators.mechanism: The bilateral differential widens from 262.5bp to 287.5bp in a single week — the widest of the cycle — precisely when the positioning squeeze has exhausted itself and the forward curve re-steepens; this is the one configuration in which both legs move against the thesis simultaneously.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CME FedWatch and TONA futures-implied probabilities for the two meetings

invalidators.condition: Brent crude sustains above $110/bbl for ten consecutive sessions on a renewed Hormuz closure
invalidators.mechanism: The pair's commodity netting is doubly asymmetric — the US gains a terms-of-trade windfall and a haven bid while Japan suffers a goods deficit widening toward JPY 1trn a month and terms of trade approaching the 69.80 record low; this is the mechanism by which the yen made a 40-year low during a war, and it overwhelms the policy channel.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Brent front-month and Hormuz commodity-ship transit counts

invalidators.condition: The combined CFTC leveraged-fund and asset-manager net yen short falls below 80,000 contracts while USD/JPY remains above 157.00
invalidators.mechanism: That is the precise signature of a squeeze that has completed without producing a trend — the fuel is spent and the price has not moved, removing the single highest-confidence input in the tactical framework and reducing the case to the guidance gap alone.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CFTC Commitments of Traders, JPY, leveraged funds plus asset managers combined
invalidators.monitor_frequency: weekly, Friday 15:30 ET as at the prior Tuesday

invalidators.condition: The Japanese 30-year JGB exceeds 4.25% while USD/JPY simultaneously trades above 161.00
invalidators.mechanism: That combination is the definitive confirmation that Japanese yields are a fiscal credit premium rather than a policy premium — the same regime that produced 95bp of bilateral ten-year compression alongside a rising pair over the past twelve months. It would void the entire strategic rate-compression thesis and reprice the pair on fiscal dominance rather than carry.

invalidators.condition: Japan's July national core CPI (20 August) prints at or below 1.4% year-on-year
invalidators.mechanism: It would confirm the core-core deceleration to 1.7% as the underlying trend, contradict the Tokyo July lead at 1.9%, and remove the BoJ's evidentiary basis for a September move — collapsing Factors 2 and 6 simultaneously, which together carry 0.21 of tactical weight.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Statistics Bureau of Japan CPI ex fresh food and ex fresh food and energy

invalidators.condition: US Treasury and MoF publicly signal that the coordinated framework will not be used again, or the late-August MoF disclosure shows the 30 July operation was below JPY 5trn
invalidators.mechanism: The pair-specific policy put — the one bilateral factor that distinguishes this analysis from a naive carry read — would be revealed as smaller and less durable than the market currently assumes, removing the asymmetry that justifies holding the view through options.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF monthly intervention disclosure and Treasury/MoF statements

signposts.confirms_if: Compresses below 250bp with the move led by the JGB two-year rising, not the US two-year falling
signposts.invalidates_if: Widens above 300bp, or compresses only because the US two-year falls on a growth scare that also crushes risk appetite
signposts.bilateral_importance: This matters more for USD/JPY than for any other pair because the two-year gap is the pure carry penalty and Japan's 2s10s at +130bp versus the US at +47bp means the front end is where all the convergence must happen. Ten-year compression has already been shown not to work for this pair.

signposts.indicator: Market-implied probability of a BoJ hike at the 18 September meeting
signposts.current_level: 23.5% on prediction markets; 38% implied by a TONA-futures bootstrap showing 62% no-change
signposts.confirms_if: Rises above 50% on both representations following the 10 August Summary of Opinions and 20 August CPI
signposts.bilateral_importance: This pair has the highest single-meeting sensitivity in the G10 because the BoJ leg is the only one of the two whose path is genuinely unpriced — the Fed's is fully discounted in bills. Each 10-percentage-point move is worth an estimated 40-60 pips.

signposts.indicator: USD/JPY spot versus the 200-day and the 155.01 structural pivot

signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's own chart, and the 155.01 level derives from the full 139.87-163.97 impulse specific to USD/JPY — no dossier TWI level substitutes for it. It is also the level at which Japanese corporate planning assumptions begin to bind.

signposts.confirms_if: Reduction of 40,000+ contracts over two consecutive reports while spot trades below 157.00 — covering driving price

signposts.bilateral_importance: Uniquely amplified in this pair because both legs are crowded the same way — specs are net long dollars and net short yen — and because the CME yen contract is the second-largest FX future, so the squeeze energy per unit of percentile extremity exceeds any cross.
signposts.frequency: weekly, Friday 15:30 ET as at the prior Tuesday

signposts.current_level: Japanese holdings ~$1.19trn (March 2026); Q1 2026 net selling of US government-linked debt $29.6bn
signposts.confirms_if: Net selling exceeds $12bn per month for two consecutive months, confirming the BoJ-tightening-to-repatriation loop is operating
signposts.invalidates_if: Japanese investors return to net buying above $5bn per month, indicating hedged Treasury economics still work at a 278bp front-end gap
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the only major FX pair where the quote-currency country holds a trillion dollars of the base-currency country's sovereign debt. The flow is pair-specific by construction and is not visible in any rate differential or positioning series.

signposts.confirms_if: Implied repricing above 9.0 with the 25-delta risk reversal deepening in favour of yen calls — the signature of genuine hedging demand for pair downside
signposts.invalidates_if: Implied falls back below 6.5 with realised converging down toward it, restoring the pre-30-July carry regime
signposts.bilateral_importance: Uniquely diagnostic for this pair because USD/JPY risk reversals are the cleanest proxy for global carry-trade vulnerability, and because the pair is the only one in the G10 where two governments transact — meaning the option surface must price a policy reaction function, not just a macro distribution.

signposts.current_level: Brent $91.82 (27 July, down from $105.32 on 23 July); Japan June mineral fuel imports JPY 2.10trn, +41.9% y/y; terms of trade 83.95
signposts.confirms_if: Brent sustained below $85, allowing Japan's July and August trade balances to narrow and terms of trade to recover above 88

signposts.bilateral_importance: Matters far more for USD/JPY than for either currency alone, because the two legs sit at opposite extremes of the energy trade — a net exporter against an economy importing 99% of its oil. The framework's netting rule makes this the single largest pair-positive force at a 0.13 strategic weight.

assumptions: Price data as source of truth: spot (157.6826, 6 August close), the 52-week range (142.11-164.088), the 71st-percentile range position, the 1M/3M/6M/1Y performance figures and all three moving averages are taken directly from the supplied Twelve Data series and were not sourced from the web.

Discrepancy flagged: the supplied 1Y performance figure of +2.31% is not reproducible from the OHLC series, which shows a close of 147.353 on 6 August 2025 against 157.6826 on 6 August 2026 — approximately +7.0%. We quote the supplied vendor figure as instructed but do not build any analysis on it.

Valuation-date versus spot-date offset: the valuation date is 2026-08-01 and both dossiers are struck at the 31 July close of 158.52, while the price series runs to 6 August at 157.6826. The 84-pip gap is immaterial to every conclusion but is disclosed rather than reconciled.

Volatility figures are partial and flagged: the last retrievable pair implied volatility is a 6.36 index print dated 28 July, two sessions before the intervention. The post-event surface was not obtainable from any public source, so all IV/VRP references likely understate current levels.

Forward points are derived, not directly quoted: the 1M/3M/6M/12M forward points are taken from the quote dossier's rebased vendor snapshot and re-rebased to the 157.6826 spot on the assumption that forward points are approximately invariant to a small spot move.

BoJ probability sources conflict and neither is suppressed: prediction-market pricing gives 23.5% for a September hike; a TONA-futures bootstrap implies roughly 38%. The 15-percentage-point gap is not reconcilable from public data and is the explicit reason Factor 1 tactical confidence is set at 50.

Intervention size is an estimate: the JPY 8.45trn / up-to-$58.97bn figure for 30 July is inferred from BoJ current-account projections and press reporting, not from an official disclosure, which is not due until late August.

Cross-currency basis is a hard gap: the 3M JPY/USD cross-currency basis — the framework's designated monitor for Factor 10 and the transmission channel for the repatriation thesis in Factor 4 — was not obtainable, for a second consecutive cycle, capping Factor 10 confidence at 48/50.
Weight adjustments: twelve individual adjustments were made across the two horizons, each within the ±0.05 limit, each with a stated bilateral reason, and each set summing to exactly 1.00.
Scenario probabilities (50/25/25 on both horizons) are analyst judgements, not derived from an options-implied distribution, because no full volatility smile was obtainable for this pair.

Bilateral trade figures in Factor 5 are used exactly as supplied from IMF DOTS (2024) and were not re-estimated or corroborated from the web; the reporting asymmetry between US and Japanese figures reflects standard CIF/FOB and timing differences and is not treated as a data error.
